**More Info**

I found that if I remove the `[ngModel]`, `(ngModelChange)`, and `<app-icon></app-icon>` from the `SearchComponent`, then the error doesn't appear.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30546713/151727707-a43c8dea-03cf-46bd-b53a-653417d30c8e.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30546713/151728582-38b8b7a5-1b81-49d0-a486-4df53d603016.png)

When calling the `createComponent()` method with `ComponentFactory`, the error doesn't appear.
I think the injected `Renderer2` in `IconComponent` is the cause of this error.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30546713/151729132-135a3d5b-d6ce-467d-adc1-9bb69d19f47a.png)

@tk2rush90 The demo link does not run on stackblitz. I also tried downloading, installing dependencies, and running with the CLI and that also didn't work. Can you please provide a working reproduction?

I was able to get the example working and reproduce the problem as described. Here's a trivial reproduction: https://stackblitz.com/edit/ng13-broken-renderer3?file=src/app.ts

It's actually a fascinating bug, and is a combination of several factors:

At the root of the issue is an assumption Angular makes: if the injector being used to create a component doesn't have a binding for `RendererFactory2`, then a factory that creates `Renderer3` (that is, `document`) is used. Exactly this happens for the dynamically instantiated component in the example. That component then attempts to inject `Renderer2`, which causes the crash.

So why is `RendererFactory2` missing? Firstly, the example app creates an injector via `Injector.create([...])`. This injector doesn't inherit from the app injector, so it doesn't have a binding for `RendererFactory2`. This didn't used to be a problem, however, since `ViewContainerRef.createComponent()` tries to create a chained injector using the given injector and the component's `NgModuleRef`. Even if the given injector was missing `RendererFactory2`, the `NgModuleRef` (usually the app injector or derived from it) would have it!

Where did the `NgModuleRef` come from? It's not common to explicitly pass that argument to `ViewContainerRef.createComponent()`. Previously that API required a `ComponentFactory`, though, which _has_ an internal `NgModuleRef` obtained from its `ComponentFactoryResolver`.

In a recent Angular though, we introduced a factory-less API for `createComponent()`, which made it easy to call the API with no `NgModuleRef`. So the _only_ tokens available for injection when creating this component are those in the user-provided injector, which does not include `RendererFactory2`. Therefore, `Renderer3` gets selected, and the component crashes!
@alxhub Thank you for helping! You're my savior!

@tk2rush90 a workaround would be to inject `Injector` inside your modal service, and use that as the base of the `Injector.create` call when you create the injector for whatever modal component is being displayed.

issue.body:
Before Ivy, it was only possible to call the `ViewContainerRef.createComponent` function with the ComponentFactory as the first argument. An instance of a `ComponentFactory` resolved via `ComponentFactoryResolver` contained a reference to an `NgModule` where the component is declared. As a result, the component maintained a DI connection with the module injector tree (by retrieving an instance of `NgModuleRef` internally), even when the custom injector was provided (we try to find a token in a custom injector first and consult module injector after that).

With Ivy, we expanded the `ViewContainerRef.createComponent` function API to support direct references to the Component classes without going through the factory resolution step. As a result, there was no connection to the NgModule that declares the component. Thus, if you provide a custom injector, this is the only injector that is taken into account.

This commit updates the logic for the factory-less case to try retrieving an instance of an `NgModuleRef` using the DI tree which `ViewContainerRef` belongs to. The `NgModuleRef` instance is then used to get a hold of a module injector tree. This brings the factory-less and factory-based logic to a consistent state.

Closes #44897.
